title: Tooth wear: erosion, abrasion, attrition & abfraction
blurb: The four kinds of tooth wear: what causes each, how to tell them apart, and the advice that protects softened enamel.
question: A 24-year-old sips cola at his desk all day and brushes hard straight after his morning orange juice. The dentist notes smooth, glassy front teeth and sharp notches at the necks of his premolars. Which kinds of tooth wear are these, and what should he be told about when to brush?

teach.body: Tooth wear (also called tooth surface loss) is the loss of enamel and dentine by processes that do NOT involve bacteria. Caries is caused by acid made by plaque bacteria from sugar. Wear is caused by acid from food, drink or the stomach, by teeth grinding together, by objects rubbing the teeth, or by teeth flexing under load. Some wear with age is normal. It becomes a problem when it is faster than expected, or causes sensitivity or changes appearance. Lost enamel never grows back.

teach.caption: Patients often have more than one type at once. Erosion softens the surface, which makes the mechanical types happen faster.

teach.body: Acid dissolves the hydroxyapatite crystals of enamel directly, softening the outer surface. Extrinsic acid comes from outside the body: fizzy drinks (diet versions too), fruit juice, squash, citrus fruit, vinegar, wine, sports drinks and effervescent tablets. Intrinsic acid is stomach acid: reflux (GORD), repeated vomiting (for example bulimia or pregnancy sickness) and heavy alcohol use. How OFTEN acid touches the teeth, and for how long, matters more than how much is drunk. Sipping and swishing keep teeth bathed in acid.

teach.h: Where erosion shows on the front teeth
teach.caption: Dietary acid tends to wear the labial (lip-side) surfaces. Stomach acid washes over the palatal surfaces of the upper teeth first, so palatal erosion is a clue to reflux or vomiting.

steps.label: Acid attack
steps.sub: An acidic drink, or vomiting, softens the enamel surface

steps.label: Rinse with water
steps.sub: Washes acid away without scrubbing the soft surface

steps.label: Wait about an hour
steps.sub: Saliva neutralises the acid and the surface starts to reharden

steps.label: Then brush
steps.sub: Fluoride toothpaste, soft or medium brush, gentle technique

teach.caption: Brushing straight after acid scrubs away the softened layer, so erosion and abrasion add together.

teach.note: If palatal erosion suggests reflux or an eating disorder, the dentist handles this sensitively and may suggest the patient sees their GP.

teach.text: The 'good habit' that harms: brushing straight after an acidic drink feels like good hygiene, but it removes softened enamel. Rinse with water, wait about an hour, then brush with fluoride toothpaste.

items: Erosion: acid without bacteria. Smooth, glassy surfaces; palatal erosion points to stomach acid.
Attrition: tooth against tooth (bruxism). Flat, shiny, matching facets.
Abrasion: an object, usually hard brushing. Sharp notches at the necks of teeth.
Abfraction: flexing under heavy load. Deep wedge at the neck, often one tooth.
Cut how often acid is taken, keep it to mealtimes, rinse and wait about an hour before brushing.

summary: You can now name the four types of tooth wear, link each to its cause and appearance, spot the clue that palatal erosion gives, and explain to a patient why they should rinse with water and wait about an hour after acid before brushing.

A.q: A patient says they brush their teeth straight after drinking fruit juice every morning. Which advice is most appropriate?
options: Brush straight away to clear the acid quickly
Rinse with water, then wait an hour to brush
Use a hard brush to scrub off the juice film
Use a whitening paste after each drink
A.why: Acid softens the enamel surface. Rinsing with water and waiting about an hour lets saliva neutralise the acid before the surface is brushed.

whyNot.0: Brushing straight away scrubs off the softened enamel, adding abrasion to erosion.
whyNot.2: A hard brush increases abrasion, especially on enamel softened by acid.
whyNot.3: Whitening pastes are often more abrasive and do nothing to reduce the acid attack.

A.q: A patient grinds their teeth at night. The dentist notes flat, shiny areas on the biting surfaces that fit exactly against the opposing teeth. Which type of wear is this?
A.why: Attrition is wear from tooth-to-tooth contact, typically from bruxism, producing matching flat facets.

whyNot.0: Erosion is chemical loss from acid; it gives smooth, rounded surfaces rather than matching facets.
whyNot.1: Abrasion is caused by an object, such as a toothbrush, not by the opposing teeth.
whyNot.3: Abfraction produces wedge-shaped lesions at the neck of the tooth, not facets on biting surfaces.

A.q: A patient has a history of repeated vomiting. Where would the dentist expect erosion to appear first?
options: Buccal surfaces of the lower molars
Labial surfaces of the lower incisors
Occlusal surfaces of the lower premolars
Palatal surfaces of upper front teeth
A.why: Stomach acid is pushed forward over the palatal surfaces of the upper teeth, so palatal erosion is the classic sign of intrinsic acid.

whyNot.0: The buccal surfaces of lower molars are not where vomited acid tends to pool first.
whyNot.1: The lower incisors are partly protected by the tongue during vomiting.
whyNot.2: Occlusal cupping can occur later, but the palatal surfaces of upper anteriors are the classic first site.

B.q: A patient drinks fizzy drinks often and brushes immediately afterwards. What is the main risk of this habit?
options: Faster build-up of plaque on the teeth
Staining being brushed into the enamel
Damage only to the gums, not the teeth
B.why: Acid softens the enamel surface, and brushing straight away wears off that softened layer.

whyNot.1: Brushing removes plaque; the harm here is to the softened tooth surface.
whyNot.2: Staining is not driven into enamel by brushing; the issue is tissue loss.
whyNot.3: Hard brushing can cause recession, but the main risk here is loss of softened enamel.

B.q: A right-handed patient who scrubs hard with a stiff brush has sharp-edged V-shaped notches at the necks of several upper left canines and premolars. Which type of wear is most likely?
B.why: Abrasion is wear from an object, most often a toothbrush used with too much force, giving sharp notches at the necks of several teeth.

whyNot.0: Attrition is tooth-to-tooth wear on biting surfaces.
whyNot.1: Erosion gives smooth, rounded, glassy surfaces rather than sharp-edged notches.
whyNot.2: Abfraction is from flexing under load, usually a single deep wedge, not a brushing pattern across several teeth.

B.q: Which of these is NOT a source of extrinsic acid?
B.why: Gastric reflux brings stomach acid up from inside the body, so it is an intrinsic cause of erosion.

whyNot.0: Diet cola is acidic even without sugar, so it is an extrinsic cause.
whyNot.1: Fruit squash contains fruit acids, an extrinsic cause.
whyNot.3: Wine is acidic and comes from outside the body, so it is extrinsic.

C.q: The dentist notes amalgam fillings standing proud of the surrounding tooth, with smooth, cupped cusps around them. Which type of wear does this suggest?
C.why: Acid dissolves tooth tissue but not the filling, so restorations end up standing proud of smooth, cupped tooth surfaces.

whyNot.0: Abrasion wears the necks of teeth where they are brushed, not the cusps around fillings.
whyNot.2: Attrition would wear the filling and the tooth flat together, leaving matching facets.
whyNot.3: Abfraction affects the neck of the tooth, not the cusps.

C.q: A single lower premolar has a deep, sharp-edged wedge at its neck. The patient brushes gently but has a very heavy bite. What is thought to cause this lesion?
options: The tooth flexing under biting load
Opposing teeth grinding down the cusp
C.why: Abfraction is thought to happen when heavy biting forces flex the tooth, so enamel and dentine crack away at the neck.

whyNot.0: Acid erosion gives smooth, rounded surfaces, not a sharp wedge on a single tooth.
whyNot.1: Sugar and bacteria cause caries, which is not a type of tooth wear.
whyNot.3: Grinding causes attrition on biting surfaces, not a wedge at the neck.

C.q: Which advice best reduces the risk of erosion?
options: Sip fizzy drinks slowly through the day
Keep acidic drinks to mealtimes only
Hold drinks in the mouth before swallowing
Brush firmly as soon as the drink is finished
C.why: Keeping acid to mealtimes cuts how often the teeth are attacked, and saliva flow is higher at meals.

whyNot.0: Sipping through the day means many separate acid attacks, the worst pattern for erosion.
whyNot.2: Holding or swishing drinks increases how long acid stays on the teeth.
whyNot.3: Brushing straight after acid wears away the softened enamel.

reteach.title: Think of a stone garden step
reteach.question: A stone step can be worn away by acid rain, by another stone grinding on it, by a scrubbing brush, or by being flexed until it cracks. Which of these matches each type of tooth wear?

blocks.h: Four ways to wear away stone
blocks.body: Acid rain slowly dissolves the surface: that is erosion, the chemical one. Two stones grinding together: that is attrition, tooth against tooth. A stiff scrubbing brush used every day: that is abrasion, an object rubbing. A step that bends a little each time someone heavy treads on it and chips at its base: that is abfraction. And acid rain makes the stone softer, so the scrubbing brush does far more damage straight after rain.

rows.label: Key advice
values: Less acid, less often; wait to brush

blocks.text: Neither erosion nor any other type of wear involves bacteria. If bacteria and sugar are the cause, it is caries, not wear.

explain.body: Acid dissolves enamel without bacteria. Dietary acid wears labial surfaces; stomach acid wears the palatal surfaces of upper teeth. Surfaces look smooth and glassy, cusps become cupped and fillings stand proud. Frequency of acid matters most.

test.q: Palatal erosion on the upper front teeth most strongly suggests which cause?
test.why: Stomach acid from reflux or vomiting flows over the palatal surfaces of the upper teeth first.

whyNot.1: Hard brushing causes abrasion, mostly at the necks of buccal surfaces.
whyNot.2: Grinding causes attrition on biting edges and cusps.
whyNot.3: Sugar feeds bacteria, causing caries rather than erosion.

explain.body: Tooth-to-tooth wear, mostly from bruxism (grinding) and clenching, often at night or under stress. It gives flat, shiny facets on incisal edges and cusp tips that match the opposing teeth. Teeth may shorten or chip. The dentist may make a bite splint (night guard) to protect them.

test.q: Which appliance might the dentist provide to protect a patient's teeth from attrition?
test.why: An occlusal splint (bite guard) worn at night stops the teeth grinding directly against each other.

whyNot.0: A gum shield protects against impact injuries in sport, not night-time grinding.
whyNot.2: A space maintainer holds a gap open after early loss of a baby tooth.
whyNot.3: A fluoride tray delivers fluoride gel; it does not stop grinding.

explain.body: Wear by an object. The usual cause is a stiff brush scrubbed side to side, sometimes with an abrasive paste. It gives sharp-edged notches at the necks of the teeth, often canines and premolars, especially where the gum has receded and softer root surface is exposed. Habits such as pipe stems or hair grips cause local notches.

explain.caption: Once the gum recedes, the root surface near the CEJ is soft and easily abraded.

test.q: Which brushing advice best helps prevent abrasion?
options: A hard brush, scrubbing firmly side to side
Gentle technique, soft or medium brush
Brushing for longer with a whitening paste
test.why: A soft or medium brush with a gentle technique cleans well without wearing the necks of the teeth.

whyNot.0: Hard brushes and side-to-side scrubbing are the main causes of abrasion.
whyNot.2: Whitening pastes can be more abrasive, and longer scrubbing increases wear.
whyNot.3: Brushing straight after acidic meals adds to wear on softened enamel.

explain.body: Abfraction is thought to happen when heavy or off-centre biting forces flex the tooth. Stress concentrates at the neck, and tiny pieces of enamel and dentine break away, forming a deep wedge with sharp edges. It often affects single teeth and can extend below the gum line.

test.q: What best distinguishes abfraction from abrasion?
options: Abfraction is caused by frequent acidic drinks
Abfraction comes from flexing, not rubbing
test.why: Both cause notches at the neck, but abfraction is thought to come from the tooth bending under load, whereas abrasion is caused by an object rubbing.

whyNot.0: Abfraction is seen in adult permanent teeth.
whyNot.3: Abfraction lesions are at the neck of the tooth, not on the biting surfaces.
